```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 15_related_anova_partitioning_variance
title: Where does it go?
questions:
  - id: slowest_person_shift
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      In a related-samples study, we take the participant who is already the
      slowest overall and add 10 seconds to all of their scores. Which sum of
      squares changes?
    options:
      - text: The between-conditions sum of squares
      - text: The between-participants sum of squares
        correct: true
      - text: The error sum of squares
    hint: >
      Does this person's pattern across the conditions change, or only their
      overall level?
    explanation: >
      This person's mean moves farther from the grand mean, so the
      between-participants sum of squares grows. Every condition mean rises by
      the same amount, so the differences among conditions don't change. And
      the person's scores all move together, so nothing changes about how they
      respond to the conditions relative to everyone else. A person's overall
      level ends up entirely in the between-participants component, which is
      why it can be taken out of the denominator.

  - id: unusual_response
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Most participants score about 5 points higher in condition B than in
      condition A, but one participant scores 5 points lower. Which component
      does that participant's unusual response contribute to?
    options:
      - text: The between-participants sum of squares
      - text: The error sum of squares
        correct: true
      - text: Neither; it is removed by the related-samples design
    explanation: >
      The related-samples design only removes a person's overall level. People
      responding differently to the conditions is left over, and so it ends up
      in the error component. That's why "error" here means more than
      measurement noise.
```
